Thanks Draven, I am now questioning whether we actually need this or not. Should we really be forcing a specific behavior even though the admin didn't want it? 

/cc @Huang-Wei @alculquicondor

> Thanks Draven, I am now questioning whether we actually need this or not. Should we really be forcing a specific behavior even though the admin didn't want it?

I think there should be some mandatory plugins that can't be disabled since the cluster can not behave correctly without them. But someone could argue the cluster-admin should be responsible for the right configuration. Both sides have their point, but I prefer we keep the mandatory behavior.

> I think there should be some mandatory plugins that can't be disabled since the cluster can not behave correctly without them. But someone could argue the cluster-admin should be responsible for the right configuration. Both sides have their point, but I prefer we keep the mandatory behavior.

The good thing about the Plugins component config API (vs the Policy API) is that it's easier to disable specific plugins, without having to re-write the whole configuration. This reduces risk of misconfiguration. Now, if an admin is specifically disabling a filter, I think we should assume that they know what they are doing. It might be trickier if they are using `*`, but we should discourage that in the documentation.

However, we can leverage this code to produce a warning, rather than forcing the plugins. Otherwise, it could be argued that we need to force the "mandatory" plugins as long as we have the Policy API. Maybe we can add them if Policy is used, but produce a warning otherwise.

> However, we can leverage this code to produce a warning, rather than forcing the plugins. Otherwise, it could be argued that we need to force the "mandatory" plugins as long as we have the Policy API. Maybe we can add them if Policy is used, but produce a warning otherwise.

Is it possible to remove the policy API after several releases? We could provide a tool or documents to guide the cluster-admin to update the configuration.

We should have clear documentation why any plugin we consider mandatory or worth a warning is essential for correct cluster behavior, why for example respecting taints and tolerations is more essential than respecting affinity?

Perhaps taint and toleration is mandatory because of "Taint Nodes by Condition" feature?

> The good thing about the Plugins component config API (vs the Policy API) is that it's easier to disable specific plugins, without having to re-write the whole configuration. This reduces risk of misconfiguration. Now, if an admin is specifically disabling a filter, I think we should assume that they know what they are doing. It might be trickier if they are using *, but we should discourage that in the documentation.

To be honest, I don't like the current disable and enable strategy. It could be quite hard for the user to figure out how to config the scheduler. Here are all the rules:

+ The custom plugin will run after the default plugins.
+ If the custom plugin should run before the default one, the default ones has to be disabled and enabled (which is quite confusing at the first time)
+ `*` could disable all the default plugins.

We could have a simpler config strategy without the "disabled plugins":

+ If the extension point of configuration is empty, use the default plugins.
+ If not, use what the admin specified and print the diff with defaults.

What do you think?

> Perhaps taint and toleration is mandatory because of "Taint Nodes by Condition" feature?

The kubelet could attach taints to the node based on the condition. When a node has taints, it always means the node can't function well now.

> We could have a simpler config strategy without the "disabled plugins":
> 
> * If the extension point of configuration is empty, use the default plugins.
> * If not, use what the admin specified and print the diff with defaults.
> 
> What do you think?

I think this has been debated already while the KEP for the framework was presented. We should respect that decision.

> Thanks Draven, I am now questioning whether we actually need this or not. Should we really be forcing a specific behavior even though the admin didn't want it?

I'm sort of against the idea of combining plugins as a new plugin - like GeneralPredicates and MandatoryPredicate we used to have. IMO it's user/admin's choices to choose which ones they want, we shouldn't behave like a "smart" guy to offer this "package" by hardcoding it in our codebase.

Instead, what we **_may_** provide is the validation logic (@damemi used to work on it) upon scheduler's startup. For instance, MostRequest and LeastReqeust Score plugins behaves in the opposite way, it's pointless to enable them together.
The other case is one plugin may depend on another (I can't think of a concrete example atm), so we can't enable a plugin without enabling its dependency.

However, sometimes the latter validation case can also be unnecessary. The chances are: users may choose to implement their own plugin to replace the in-tree plugin. For example, there is a long-discussed topic about scheduling Pods based on dynamic node utilization. In this case, users can choose to not enable the in-tree "noderesouce" plugin; instead, enable their out-of-tree plugin, based on node metrics.

So, my point is:

- don't define new plugin by just simply combining existing plugins
- don't define any plugin as mandatory
- with validation logic, also be cautious - validate whatever really needs to be validated

---

This reminds me of another thing similar. We can enforce some extension point (e.g. QueueSort) as mandatory, but we can't say the default in-tree PrioritySort plugin (based on .spec.priorityValue) is mandatory.

issue_context.title: Support mandatory plugins in the scheduling framework
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:

Add mandatory plugins that can't be removed from the default plugins.

**Why is this needed**:

We have mandatory predicates that should be configured all the time, and we still need them when migrates to scheduling plugins.

```go
		// MandatoryPredicates the set of keys for predicates that the scheduler will
		// be configured with all the time.
		MandatoryPredicates: sets.NewString(
			predicates.PodToleratesNodeTaintsPred,
			predicates.CheckNodeUnschedulablePred,
		),
```

/sig scheduling
/priority important-soon

> + don't define new plugin by just simply combining existing plugins
> + don't define any plugin as mandatory
> + with validation logic, also be cautious - validate whatever really needs to be validated

review_comments: @ahg-g I've added several unit tests here. Do we still need the compatibility test?
The compatibility test tests the configuration behavior of predicates and priorities.

The compatibility test should verify the behavior of the configuration API, not just the Policy API. In this case, the test would verify that if the configuration didn't specify those filters, they should still be included in the final scheduler configuration.

> The compatibility test should verify the behavior of the configuration API, not just the Policy API. In this case, the test would verify that if the configuration didn't specify those filters, they should still be included in the final scheduler configuration.

I see your point. What I mean is, all of the tests are for predicates and priorities, do we need to create tests with plugin configuration in the compatibility tests now?
Yes, we should have compatibility tests now for plugin-based configurations.

> Yes, we should have compatibility tests now for plugin-based configurations.

Sure, can I open another PR to update the compatibility tests first since we have not reached a consensus on what we should do with mandatory plugins?
